description: Somos un equipo apasionado por la ciencia, la tecnología y la exploración espacial. En el NASA Space Apps Challenge, unimos nuestras ideas, creatividad y conocimientos para desarrollar soluciones innovadoras a desafíos reales. ¡Exploramos, creamos e innovamos juntos!
summary: The Integrated Spaceflight Intra-Habitat Health & Environmental Monitoring System is an advanced bioastronautics platform designed to support long-duration space exploration, such as multi-year missions to Mars, where communication latencies with Earth exceed twenty minutes. To balance astronaut operational autonomy with centralized clinical oversight, the software employs a dual-perspective framework encompassing an astronaut crew perspective for local, low-friction self-monitoring and a ground medical team perspective for telemetry and longitudinal evaluation. The platform integrates eight core functional modules—covering physiological telemetry, sleep, nutrition, environmental radiation, AI health analysis, automated medical alerts, biological biomarkers, and psychological well-being—into a Central Cross-Correlation Engine to detect non-linear performance deviations and mitigate NASA's Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight. Operating independently during communication blackouts, the system utilizes modular hardware like ESP32 microcontrollers and BME280 sensors while enforcing strict safety protocols, including AES-256 encrypted psychological journals, alarm fatigue triage, and mandatory physician-in-the-loop validation for countermeasure deployment. By unifying previously siloed diagnostic streams into a single resilient architecture, the platform preserves clinical context, enhances crew safety, and advances long-term space biology research.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

In long-duration spaceflight such as multi-year transits to Mars or sustained human presence beyond Low Earth Orbit (LEO), the operational architecture of bioastronautics monitoring software must address the distinct environments of deep-space crews and terrestrial ground control. Communication latencies, ranging from several seconds at the Moon to over twenty minutes each way during Martian transits, eliminate the possibility of real-time clinical tele-operation from Earth. Consequently, the software architecture is bifurcated into a dual-perspective framework (Canadian Space Agency, 2025; Russell et al., 2023).

This dual-perspective architecture balances crew operational autonomy with centralized clinical oversight. The Astronaut Crew Perspective prioritizes crew self-monitoring, cognitive load management, and immediate actionable feedback without inducing diagnostic distraction or alarm fatigue during complex intra-vehicular activities. Conversely, the Space Station and Ground Medical Team Perspective provides Earth-based Flight Surgeons and Mission Control Data Integration Specialists with deep telemetry, historical baseline overlays, and multi-system analytical modeling tools. Differentiating these interfaces ensures that in-flight operators retain localized self-awareness while ground-based medical teams preserve macro-level diagnostic oversight.

Regarding feature and attribute breakdown across perspectives, the Astronaut Crew Perspective focuses on low-friction self-monitoring, rapid task execution, cognitive load minimization, high-level summary dashboards, simplified status indicators, actionable countermeasure alerts, localized task readiness scores, individual profile access, self-entry logging interfaces, encrypted personal psychological journals, and local environment readouts. It operates fully offline to maintain continuous execution during communication latency and blackout phases. In contrast, the Space Station and Ground Medical Team Perspective focuses on comprehensive longitudinal clinical evaluation, multi-system anomaly diagnosis, fleet-wide health archives, raw biometric streams, multi-channel EEG and NIRS outputs, multi-omics profiles, full environmental telemetry, sub-threshold signal spectrums, historical baseline overlays, and asynchronous delay-tolerant batch data processing queues.

These operational perspectives interact through continuous background data synchronization mechanisms. Telemetry gathered at the crew interface feeds into the system’s central processing modules, establishing the operational foundation for both onboard real-time self-monitoring and ground-based medical tele-oversight.

Furthermore, transitioning from basic asynchronous queues to standardized Delay-Tolerant Networking protocols ensures robust packet exchange and reliable data synchronization between orbital stations and terrestrial ground bases across massive interplanetary distances.

The platform integrates eight core functional modules designed for shirt-sleeve intra-vehicular environment operation without requiring extravehicular activity suits. All modules feed into a Central Cross-Correlation Engine:

First, the Astronaut Health Overview module handles continuous collection of physiological parameters, including heart rate variability, respiration rate, core body temperature, and physical activity intensity via chest-wearable ECG and actigraphy. It links wearable sensors over a low-power wireless network topology while evaluating autonomic nervous system equilibrium during routine and high-stress mission phases.

Second, the Sleep and Circadian Monitoring module tracks total sleep duration, sleep continuity, and sleep stage architecture through wrist actigraphy and polysomnography. It monitors circadian entrainment using markers such as urinary 6-sulphatoxymelatonin, core body temperature rhythms, and targeted light-exposure logging to minimize circadian misalignment.

Third, the Nutrition and Hydration module interfaces with intra-habitat supply databases to log daily caloric intake, macro-nutrient distributions, fluid consumption, B-vitamin profiles, folate, L-methylfolate, vitamin B-12, methylmalonic acid, and homocysteine to mitigate risks associated with Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome.

Fourth, the Space Environment and Internal Habitat Monitoring module continuously logs ionizing radiation exposure (measuring Galactic Cosmic Ray exposure, high-Z and high-energy ion flux, and particle events) while tracking ambient habitat parameters including partial pressure of carbon dioxide, barometric pressure, ambient temperature, and relative humidity.

Fifth, the AI Health Analysis module uses algorithmic engines to fuse parallel streams of physiological data, environmental telemetry, actigraphy, and cognitive performance scores, identifying early-stage multi-system anomalies and non-linear performance deviations that escape isolated univariate threshold monitoring.

Sixth, the Medical Alerts and Out-of-Bounds Threshold Management module compares real-time bio-telemetry against dynamic reference bands, flagging out-of-bounds parameters instantly, generating automated alerts for ground-based Flight Surgeons, and maintaining a tamper-evident audit history.

Seventh, the Biomarker and Biological Sample Monitoring module manages assay data derived from saliva, hair, blood, and urine samples. It logs stress hormones, inflammatory cytokines, matrix metalloproteinases, Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein, Neurofilament Light Chain, phospho-tau 181, beta-amyloid ratios, 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine, and microRNA profiles, linking sample data directly with physiological telemetry.

  • Eighth, the Psychological Health and Well-being Monitoring module administers regular neurobehavioral batteries such as the Psychomotor Vigilance Test, provides an encrypted private journal subsystem using local natural language processing to extract sub-clinical emotional regulation metrics, and evaluates stress indices alongside Default Mode Network neuroimaging metrics (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 2023).

Data generated by these functional modules flows into the system's multisystem data correlation engine. The engine integrates environmental streams (such as elevated ambient CO2 and radiation background), behavioral streams (such as decreased psychomotor speed and response variability), and physiological streams (such as elevated cortisol, cytokines, and sleep fragmentation) to generate non-causal risk notifications like "Elevated Cognitive Fatigue Risk".

This non-causal methodology relies on NASA Human Research Program findings regarding Combined Behavioral Stressors, recognizing that simultaneous exposures to particle radiation, microgravity fluid shifts, atmospheric carbon dioxide elevations, and sleep fragmentation interact non-linearly at the neural circuit level to degrade executive function, spatial orientation, and operational reaction time (Russell et al., 2023).

Relying solely on real-time human approval from Earth fails during Martian transits or complete communication blackouts where signal delays exceed twenty minutes. Integrating local onboard decision rules empowers the onboard crew medical officer to authorize critical countermeasures independently when communication links sever entirely.

2. What benefits does it have?

The system provides significant clinical and operational benefits through longitudinal health optimization by baseline comparison. Broad population-wide reference ranges used in terrestrial clinical medicine are often insufficient for assessing astronaut populations exposed to microgravity, space radiation, and closed environments. By evaluating continuous in-flight telemetry against individualized pre-flight reference baselines rather than static population averages, the individual deviation model isolates true physiological shifts from inherent baseline variations (Antonsen et al., 2023).

Additionally, the platform delivers medically validated countermeasure and lifestyle recommendations through a structured feedback workflow. Recommendations generated by the algorithmic engine enter a pending validation queue where they are blocked from crew view until reviewed and approved by a NASA Flight Surgeon. Approved countermeasures are then deployed to the crew action schedule, and post-execution biometric feedback is ingested back into the system to refine dynamic baseline models (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 2023).

Finally, the platform ensures mission-wide medical evolution preservation by acting as a centralized repository for every crew member’s longitudinal health timeline. By continuously archiving raw and processed biometric streams, environmental exposure logs, biological assay records, and countermeasure responses, the system prevents diagnostic fragmentation and preserves complete clinical context across multi-year exploration missions.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The system is designed to directly mitigate spaceflight hazards during deep-space exploration transits across NASA's Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight framework (Antonsen et al., 2023). For Space Radiation, the platform continuously logs radiation background and DNA damage markers to map exposure budgets and trigger dietary or shielding protocols. For Isolation and Confinement, it processes encrypted journals, psychomotor vigilance tasks, and social stress markers to detect early emotional dysregulation and adjust crew workloads. For Distance from Earth, it provides an autonomous local multi-stream correlation engine and diagnostic database to enable autonomous onboard medical support without real-time Earth reliance. For Altered Gravity Fields, it tracks postural sway, vestibulo-ocular reflexes, and motor performance to optimize exercise countermeasures and operational readiness. For Hostile/Closed Environments, it monitors habitat CO2, pressure, humidity, and thermal telemetry against NASA-STD-3001 limits to identify atmospheric parameter spikes before acute clinical symptoms manifest (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 2023, 2026).

Beyond immediate crew performance enhancement, the high-resolution bio-telemetry datasets recorded by the platform advance long-term space biology research. These datasets inform ground-based translational models, enhance the translatability of animal research paradigms to human spaceflight contexts, and provide empirical engineering parameters for designing next-generation exploration hardware and habitat habitability envelopes.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?The system integrates research databases and operational frameworks from NASA's Human Research Program and the Canadian Space Agency (Canadian Space Agency, 2025). It incorporates NASA HRP risk matrices, permissible exposure limits, and combined behavioral stressor datasets. It also ingests CSA operational radiation algorithms, dosimetric translation models, and bio-dosimetry blood marker indicators (specifically FLT3LG, SAA1, C3, and VCAM-1). Furthermore, ground-to-orbit research translation frameworks map animal testing paradigms (such as 5-Choice Continuous Performance Testing and Morris Water Maze navigation) to human behavioral batteries like Psychomotor Vigilance Testing and virtual maze perspective-taking tasks.

The software architecture enforces full compliance with NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2 (Human Factors, Habitability, and Environmental Health) (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 2026). It integrates habitability and spatial volume constraints from Sections 8.1 through 8.4 governing net habitable volume, configuration efficiency, translation paths, and doorway clearances. It embeds material thermal inertia limits (Table 23) to calculate permissible material touch temperatures between 0°C and 49°C based on material inverse thermal inertia and expected contact duration. It also sets strict atmospheric limits including maximum CO2 partial pressure (pCO2 below 3.0 mmHg nominal), total barometric pressure, acoustic noise exposure envelopes, and ambient thermal stability.

The physical hardware deployment centers on an ESP32 microcontroller powered by a 18650 rechargeable battery connected via the VIN pin (Cavicchioli et al., 2021; De Martino et al., 2026; Fei et al., 2010). The microcontroller collects environmental telemetry via a BME280 sensor (reading humidity, temperature, and atmospheric pressure using I2C communication on GPIO pins 21 and 22), detects motion via a flexible sensor (Flex-S) on pin GPIO 32, and measures heart rate via a HW-827 pulse sensor connected to pin GPIO 34. Collected data is displayed locally on an OLED screen and transmitted wirelessly via IP address server architecture to mobile devices.

The physical prototype accompanying the software bridges the gap between digital architecture and physical reality. Built with modular hardware components—such as the ESP32 microcontroller, BME280 environmental sensors, and pulse monitoring modules—the prototype operationalizes theoretical bio-monitoring concepts. This tangible model moves ideas beyond the screen and mental frameworks into a concrete, functioning artifact that demonstrates real-time data acquisition and local telemetry display.

5. How is your project creative?

Historically, spaceflight medical operations relied on siloed, single-purpose hardware devices and standalone software packages where biometrics, dietary logging, environmental telemetry, and psychological assessments were recorded across disparate systems. The platform's primary architectural innovation is the consolidation of these isolated streams into a single unified monitoring platform (Canadian Space Agency, 2025; De Martino et al., 2026). By combining physiological telemetry, nutritional tracking, environmental data, multi-omics biomarkers, AI multi-stream correlation, and psychological metrics within one system, the platform reduces crew cognitive friction and provides a unified flight surgeon dashboard.

Furthermore, the project introduces bi-directional dual-perspective operational synergy (Canadian Space Agency, 2025). The Astronaut Crew Perspective handles local data ingest, rapid diagnostic entry, self-awareness, and countermeasure execution views, while the Space Station and Ground Control Perspective manages macro-level telemetry, trend evaluation, hazard modeling, and countermeasure authorization. A bi-directional synchronization layer featuring delay-tolerant data exchange links these two perspectives to form a closed-loop health tracking architecture.

6. What factors did your team consider?

The development team accounted for precision calibration and microgravity-induced physiological shifts, adjusting raw telemetry against profile-specific expected baseline ranges customized to each crew member using formal multi-variable mathematical models that factor in pre-flight baseline values, age, sex, fluid redistribution time constants, cumulative radiation exposure, radiogenic adaptation functions, and intra-individual variance (Antonsen et al., 2023).

The team also incorporated medical alert threshold limits and algorithmic rigor to prevent alarm fatigue (Russell et al., 2023). Incoming bio-telemetry passes through dynamic baseline filters and is triaged into three levels: routine physiological fluctuations (logged silently in the background), sub-clinical trend alerts (routed to the flight surgeon queue for review), and critical clinical emergencies (triggering immediate crew and ground alarms).

To protect crew privacy, psychological privacy frameworks and data security were designed into the architecture. Private journal entries are encrypted locally on crew devices using AES-256 protocols. A local natural language processing engine analyzes text on-device to extract anonymized emotional regulation index metrics without exposing raw text entries to ground control or mission management.

Finally, a mandatory physician-in-the-loop validation protocol ensures that algorithmic recommendations (such as dietary, supplementation, or lifestyle changes) generated by AI engines are held in a pending queue. These actions are intercepted and blocked from crew view until a qualified NASA Flight Surgeon evaluates the data and approves deployment to the crew schedule.

While commercial-off-the-shelf components like standard microcontrollers and 18650 cells serve effectively for terrestrial desktop mockups, deep-space missions demand radiation-hardened microcontrollers and redundant circuitry. Factoring in ionizing radiation prevents premature hardware degradation and ensures continuous operational reliability during multi-year interplanetary transits.

Additionally, lithium-ion batteries present severe thermal management risks within closed, pressurized space habitats due to potential off-gassing, electrolyte leakage, or fire hazards in microgravity. Mandating strict cell containment protocols and aerospace-grade suppression systems safeguards both habitat structural integrity and crew health.
